newsitem.title: UK: UK's Diana gets ministry go-ahead for Bosnia visit.
newsitem.headline: UK's Diana gets ministry go-ahead for Bosnia visit.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana will fly to Bosnia to crusade against landmines and the foreign office on Tuesday gave her the security go-ahead for the controversial visit.
Diana, who launched her anti-landmine campaign with a high profile visit in January to Angola on behalf of the Red Cross, was expected to leave for Bosnia at the end of the week.

Her intention to visit Bosnia coincided with a flurry of political and diplomatic pressure on the country's factions to hand over war-crime suspects and force a fair division of diplomatic posts by its ethnically split government.
A Foreign Office spokesman said it welcomed Diana's involvement in the landmine issue and the impetus it had given to the international campaign to get them banned.
"We have undertaken a security assessment. Our advice at this stage to the Princess of Wales is to go ahead. But we are of course keeping the security situation under close review."
Her office had earlier confirmed Diana's intention "to make a private visit (to Bosnia) in the near future".
But the Red Cross said it knew nothing about the planned Bosnia trip.
"If she is going to Bosnia she is not going with the Red Cross. We don't know who she is going with. It is very confusing. We haven't got a clue what is going on," said a British Red Cross spokesman.
The 36-year-old princess launched her anti-mine campaign in January with a high profile visit to Angola on behalf of the Red Cross.

Two weeks ago she was forced to scrap a planned trip to Bosnia for the Red Cross, apparently because of the embarrassment of a possible meeting with Ljiljana Karadzic -- wife of indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic. Mrs Karadzic is president of the Bosnian Serb Republic's branch of the Red Cross.
The organisation said on Tuesday it had decided that a visit to Bosnia by the princess would not have been right because of the overall political and security situation.

British troops last month led a swoop on two Serbs suspected of war crimes, angering ultra-nationalist Serbs and provoking retaliatory bombings against international monitors and NATO peacekeeping troops in Bosnia.
The news of Diana's planned private trip came as Britain and other Western countries toughened policy towards Bosnia over its failure to meet peace treaty deadlines.

A handful of major Western states have suspended contacts with the Bosnian ambassador to London because Bosnian leaders had failed to meet an August 1 deadline for the joint Moslem-Serb-Croat presidency to agree on the appointment of ambassadors.
The United States, Germany, France, Italy, Sweden and other European allies are concerned by the slowdown in efforts to implement Bosnia's 1995 peace treaty.
Diana's trip to Angola was her first working trip abroad since her divorce in August 1996 from heir to the throne Prince Charles.
Some British parliamentarians accused Diana of meddling in international affairs, but the Angola visit strengthened her desire to be a "queen of hearts" or informal ambassador for Britain.

Her apparent determination to undertake the trip despite the apparent drawbacks follows hostile media coverage of her glitzy holiday in the south of France last month as a guest of the Egyptian-born owner of London's Harrods department store.
